title: Meeting and greeting each other
goal: Talk about what people do together and to each other. Extend the *ber-* verbs you met in A1, learn the reciprocal *ber-…-an* (*bersalaman, berpelukan*) and the all-purpose *saling*, and hear how friends shorten them to *salaman, pacaran, ketemuan*.
bekal: describe meetings and greetings: *bertemu, berjumpa, bersalaman, berpelukan*
say “each other” two ways: *saling membantu* and *berpelukan*
count people with *ber-*: *berdua, bertiga* — and make a plan to *ketemuan*

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Syukuran kantor baru
dialogs.intro: Friday afternoon. The Yogyakarta office holds a *syukuran*, a small thanksgiving gathering to mark its official opening, three months after it quietly started work. Pak Hendra, Sarah's old boss from Jakarta and now regional head, has flown in for it.

lines.text: Mbak Sarah, ayo ke depan. Pak Hendra sudah datang dari Jakarta.
lines.id: Sarah, come to the front. Pak Hendra's arrived from Jakarta.
lines.literal: Miss Sarah, come-on to front. Mr Hendra already come from Jakarta.

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Oh ya? Sudah lama sekali kami tidak bertemu.
lines.id: Has he? We haven't seen each other for ages.
lines.literal: oh yes? already long very we not meet.

lines.speaker: Hendra:
lines.text: Sarah! Apa kabar? Akhirnya kita bertemu lagi, di Yogya pula.

lines.literal: Sarah! what news? finally we meet again, in Yogya moreover.

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Kabar baik, Pak. Senang sekali bisa berjumpa lagi dengan Bapak.

lines.text: Baik. Tumpengnya sudah siap, Mbak Nur?
lines.id: Right. Is the tumpeng ready, Mbak Nur?

lines.text: Sudah, Pak. Nanti Bapak yang memotong tumpeng, lalu kita berdoa bersama.

lines.text: Tenang, Mas. Hari ini saya berdiri di depan.

lines.text: Bagus. Kantor ini masih kecil, jadi kita harus saling membantu.
lines.id: Good. This office is still small, so we must all help each other.

notes: **Syukuran** is a thanksgiving gathering held to mark a new start: a new office, a new house, a new job, a recovery. There is a short prayer, a speech or two, and food, almost always including a *tumpeng*. The word comes from *syukur*, gratitude — the same root as *syukurlah*, “thank goodness”.

**Bertemu, berjumpa, ketemu.** All three mean “to meet”. *Bertemu* is the standard word, *berjumpa* is a notch more formal and literary (you know it from *Sampai jumpa*), and 💬 *ketemu* is what everyone says in conversation. *Di Yogya pula* — *pula* adds “on top of that, of all things”.

**Bersalaman.** Sarah and Pak Hendra shake hands, not hug. Between a man and a woman, and between a boss and a staff member, the handshake is the safe and warm choice. Some people, especially devout Muslims, prefer not to touch the opposite sex at all; they touch their hand to their chest instead, and you simply do the same.

**Saling kenal.** *Saling* before a verb means “each other”, and it works with almost anything: *saling kenal*, *saling membantu*, *saling menjaga*, *saling percaya*. The verb after *saling* can be bare (*kenal*) or in its *me-* form (*membantu*); both are normal.

**Mohon maaf, Bapak, Mbak.** Mbak Nur interrupts her superior in the most correct way possible: an apology first, then everyone addressed by title, then the information as a passive (*dimulai*). It sounds stiff in translation; in Indonesian it simply sounds professional.

**Tumpeng** is a cone of yellow or white rice surrounded by side dishes. The most senior person cuts off the tip and hands it to someone they wish to honour, often the oldest person present. Pak Hendra will be expected to make a small speech while he does it.

grammars.title: ber- beyond the basics
body: In A1 you met *ber-* in *bekerja, belajar, berenang*. The prefix has a broader job: it makes verbs of doing something on your own or with others, of having or wearing something, and of being in a group. None of them takes an object.

head: ber- word
Root
English
Kind
rows: the two, the three of us

after: *ber-* loses its *r* before a root that begins with *r* (*berenang* from *renang*) and in the single word *bekerja*; it becomes *bel-* only in *belajar*. Everywhere else it is *ber-*.
⚠️ *Berfoto* means to pose for a photo. To take a photo of something is *memotret* or 💬 *foto* on its own: *Tolong fotoin, Mas* in Jakarta, *Tolong difoto, Mas* anywhere.

grammars.title: Each other: ber-…-an and saling
body: Indonesian has two ways of saying that people do something to each other. *ber-…-an* wraps round a small set of roots, mostly about touching and relationships; *saling* goes before any verb.

head: ber-…-an
English
saling + verb
English
rows: to look out for each other

after: You can say *Mereka saling berpelukan*, and many Indonesians do, but careful editors call it double work, since *ber-…-an* already means “each other”. *Mereka berpelukan* is enough.
Neither form needs a pronoun after it. English says “they hugged each other”; Indonesian says *mereka berpelukan* and stops.

dialogs.title: Second dialogue — Kabar dari Rina
dialogs.intro: That evening Rina rings from Jakarta. She sounds suspiciously happy.

lines.speaker: Rina:
lines.text: Sar, aku mau cerita. Kamu lagi sibuk nggak?
lines.id: Sar, I've got news. Are you busy?
lines.literal: Sar, I want tell. you in-the-middle busy not?

lines.text: Nggak, kok. Ada apa? Suaramu senang banget.
lines.id: No, not at all. What's up? You sound really happy.
lines.literal: no, [kok]. exist what? voice-your happy very.

lines.speaker: Rina:

lines.text: Kayaknya iya. Waktu dia pulang dari Surabaya, kami berpelukan di bandara kayak di film.
lines.id: Looks like it. When he got back from Surabaya we hugged at the airport like in a film.
lines.literal: seems yes. time he return from Surabaya, we hug-each-other at airport like in film.

lines.text: Romantis banget! Kalian nggak pernah bertengkar?
lines.id: How romantic! Don't you two ever argue?

lines.text: Pernah, dong. Tapi kami selalu cepat baikan.

lines.speaker: Rina:
lines.text: Iya, Bu Guru. Eh, kapan kamu main ke Jakarta? Nanti kita ketemuan, ya!
lines.id: Yes, Miss. Hey, when are you coming to Jakarta? We'll meet up, OK?
lines.literal: yes, Mrs Teacher. hey, when you play to Jakarta? later we meet-up, yes!

lines.text: Pasti. Kita bertiga ketemuan, biar aku bisa kenal Andi lebih dekat.
lines.id: Definitely. The three of us should meet, so I can get to know Andi better.

notes: **Sar.** Friends clip names to one syllable, usually the first: *Sar* for Sarah, *Rin* for Rina, *Bay* for Bayu. Between Sarah and Rina it is *aku* and *kamu* throughout; *saya* would sound as if they had quarrelled.
**Ketemu orang tuaku. Resmi!** Meeting the parents “officially” is a real step in Indonesia: it usually means marriage is being discussed. Watch for the next stage, the *lamaran*, later in this book.

**Pacaran** is the spoken form of *berpacaran*, “to be going out together”, from *pacar*, boyfriend or girlfriend. 💬 Conversation drops the *ber-* from most *ber-…-an* words: *pacaran, kenalan, salaman, pelukan, baikan, ketemuan*.

**Kayaknya** is the spoken *sepertinya*, “it seems, looks like”. With *banget* (very), *udah* (*sudah*) and *nggak* (*tidak*), Rina's lines are a perfect sample of relaxed Jakarta speech. In writing, all four go back to their standard forms.
**Bertengkar, baikan.** *Bertengkar* is to quarrel, and it is already reciprocal without *-an*. Making up is *berbaikan*, spoken *baikan*, from *baik*: to become good with each other again.

**Iya, Bu Guru** — “yes, Miss”. When a friend starts giving advice, Indonesians tease them by calling them *Bu Guru* or *Pak Ustaz* (religious teacher). Sarah has been moralising, and Rina lets her know it, affectionately.

grammars.title: The spoken -an words
body: In conversation, reciprocal and social verbs lose their *ber-* and keep the *-an*. Some roots that never take *ber-…-an* in standard Indonesian get *-an* in speech anyway, like *ketemuan*.

head: Spoken
Standard
English
rows: to get to know each other
to make up after a quarrel

after: ⚠️ Some of these are also ordinary nouns: *kenalan* is an acquaintance, *pelukan* is a hug (*pelukan hangat*, a warm hug). Context sorts it out.
💬 *Bareng* is the everyday word for *bersama* all over Java: *makan bareng, pulang bareng*.

blocks.text: Greeting with the body matters in Indonesia, and the rules depend on age, gender and closeness. Here is what you will see, and what it means.

blocks.text: The handshake is gentle, not a grip, and it is often followed by bringing your right hand briefly to your chest: “from the heart”. When a child like Dimas starts to *salim* to you, you know you have become family.
*ber-* plus a number tells you how many people are doing something together. It is the natural answer to *Berapa orang?* when you arrive at a restaurant, too.
